verses.translation_literal: To the choirmaster, to the sons of Korah, a psalm.
verses.translation_dramatic: For the choirmaster, from the sons of Korah: a psalm.
verses.directors_commentary:
This line is not part of the poem; it is the label that was hung on it, and the label tells us how the psalm was used. "To the choirmaster" (lamnaṣṣēaḥ) is the formula that opens fifty-five psalms. The word comes from a root meaning to oversee or lead; the ancients understood it as the director of the Temple music, and the Targum reads it as "to praise". "Sons of Korah" are the Levitical guild of singers who kept the gates and the choirs; their name is attached to eleven psalms, 49 among them. "A psalm" is mizmôr, a song sung with stringed instruments, which matters here, because the poet will say in verse 5 that he opens his riddle on the harp.

The KJV prints "A Psalm for the sons of Korah" as an unnumbered heading and starts counting at the next line, which is why every verse in this chapter is one number higher in the Hebrew. The preposition le can mean "for", "to" or "by"; the KJV took it as "for", and the Hebrew does not decide. Ibn Ezra and Radak both treat this as a poem for everyone, for "every people" and "anyone who wants the good path", not a private prayer. Direct accordingly: this is a public performance.

philological_notes.note: "To the choirmaster": a participle of the root that means to be pre-eminent or to oversee. The traditional meaning of a musical director is the one the Targum and the KJV ("chief Musician") follow; it is a performance direction, not part of the poem.
"To/for the sons of Korah", the descendants of the Levite Korah, a guild of Temple singers. The preposition le is ambiguous between dedication and authorship.

verses.translation_literal: Hear this, all the peoples; give ear, all the inhabitants of [the] world.
verses.translation_dramatic: Hear this, all you peoples. Listen well, every one of you who lives in the world.
verses.directors_commentary:
Wisdom poems usually address a pupil ("my son"). Here the speaker turns to the whole earth, which is an extraordinary stage direction: the singer stands before the Temple crowd and calls over their heads to every nation. The commentators agree that this is the point. Rashi says all peoples are called because all of them need this instruction, and Ibn Ezra says it reaches every living thing into which God breathed the breath of life. Nothing in the psalm is about Israel's law; its subject, death, belongs to everyone.

The KJV's "all ye people" is a small blur: Hebrew has the plural 'ammîm, "peoples" in the sense of nations, which YLT and ASV restore. Two near-synonyms for listening open the verse, "hear" and "give ear", the second a verb built from the word for ear (ʾōzen), so the Hebrew literally says "ear this". And ḥāled, "world", is a rare word, used only in poetry, with a sense close to "the passing age" (Metzudat Zion glosses it as "people of the time", and Rashi derives it from the word for something that wears away). The poet chose the one word for the world that already hints it will not last.

philological_notes.note: A poetic word for the world, found a handful of times in the Bible (Ps 17:14; 89:48; Isa 38:11). Rashi connects it with wearing away; Metzudat Zion glosses it as people of the time. The sense of 'the passing age' fits the psalm's theme.
"Give ear": a verb made from the noun 'ear' (ʾōzen), literally 'to ear' something.

verses.translation_literal: Both sons of Adam, both sons of man (ʾîš), together rich and needy.
verses.translation_dramatic: Commoner and nobleman alike, the rich beside the beggar, the whole crowd of you, side by side.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalmist widens the circle from every nation (verse 2) to every rank, and he does it with a pair of near-synonyms that Hebrew hears as a deliberate contrast. Běnê ʾādām, 'sons of Adam', is the crowd, ordinary humanity; běnê ʾîš, 'sons of man', is the person of standing, the sort of man a name is attached to. Meiri, Radak and Metzudat Zion all read the pair this way (the mass of people against the great or the wise), and the second pair, 'rich and needy', then restates it in money terms. The same pairing sits in Psalm 62:10 (62:9 in English), where it again means low against high.

The KJV, with the ASV and Webster after it, renders the pair 'low and high'. That takes the sense the commentators give, and it is a fair reading, but it costs the sound and the root-play: Adam, the earth-creature, set against ʾîš, the man with a place in society. Both are the same human being; only the rank differs. The closing 'together' (yaḥad) is the point of the whole psalm: this teaching is for everyone at once, because death, as the next verses will say, does not separate them. Stage it as a speaker turning to a packed gate, where the rich stand at the front and the poor at the back, and addressing both ends of the room.

philological_notes.note: Two words for 'human' in parallel, with ʾādām as the common run of people and ʾîš as the person of rank. The doubled gam ('both … both') stresses that no one is left out. The KJV's 'low and high' keeps the contrast but drops the wordplay between the two nouns.
'Together', 'alike': rich and needy are gathered in one place to hear. Metzudat David glosses it 'this one like that one', putting the stress on equality.

verses.translation_literal: My mouth will speak wisdoms, and the murmuring of my heart [will be] understandings.
verses.translation_dramatic: My mouth will speak wisdom. And what my heart has been murmuring in the dark will come out as understanding.
verses.directors_commentary:
The poet announces his credentials in two parallel halves: mouth and heart, what is said aloud and what has been turned over inwardly. The second noun, hāgût, comes from the root hgh, which is the sound of low murmuring: it is used of a dove's moan and of the quiet repeating of Torah in Psalm 1 ("he meditates"). "Meditation", the KJV's choice, is right but too tidy, and loses the sense of muttering to oneself. Metzudat David adds a fine touch: besides the words that everyone will hear, there are hidden things in what the poet thinks.

Both key words are plural, and the Hebrew keeps them that way: ḥokmôt, "wisdoms" (the intensive plural, as in Proverbs 1:20, where Wisdom is a woman crying in the street), and tĕbûnôt, "understandings". The KJV flattens both to the singular. Ibn Ezra notes this is wisdom that is hidden, and the sages "tell it by way of riddle", which prepares for the next verse.

philological_notes.note: 'Murmuring, meditation': from the root of low sounds such as a dove's moan or the muttering over a text. The rendering 'murmuring' keeps the physical sound that 'meditation' loses.
Plural of ḥokmâ, 'wisdom'; used elsewhere for personified Wisdom. The plural is a plural of fullness and I keep it as a plural in the literal layer.

verses.translation_literal: I will incline my ear to a proverb; I will open my riddle with a harp.
verses.translation_dramatic: I will bend my ear to a proverb first, and then, over the strings of the harp, I will unlock my riddle.
verses.directors_commentary:
The poet is a listener before he is a speaker: he bends his ear to the proverb, as if wisdom were something he receives, and only then plays. Meiri reads it this way, as the poet teaching himself first and others afterwards, and Metzudat David makes the same point, that he warns himself too and not only others. This is the posture of a prophet-singer: oracles in Israel were sometimes accompanied by music (compare 2 Kings 3:15, where Elisha asks for a harpist before speaking).

The key words are "proverb" (māšāl) and "riddle" (ḥîdâ). The KJV's "parable" and "dark saying" are respectable, but "dark saying" is odd English, and ḥîdâ is the word for Samson's riddle at his wedding (Judges 14): a sealed puzzle with an answer. That is why the verb is "open" (ʾeptaḥ), which means to unlock something closed. Radak notes that the Psalms were sung to harp and lyre, so the poem itself is the performance; Metzudat David adds that the music makes the meaning clear. Rashi points at what the riddle is: the question of the next verse. Direct the harp to be heard under the words.

philological_notes.note: 'My riddle': a closed saying that requires opening. The same noun names Samson's wedding riddle (Judges 14). KJV 'dark saying' is a paraphrase of this sense.
'I will open': the verb that fits a closed riddle, an unsealed puzzle.
A hand-held lyre or harp, the standard instrument of the Levitical singers. The poem is to be sung to it.

verses.translation_literal: Why should I fear in days of evil, [when] the iniquity of my heels surrounds me?
verses.translation_dramatic: Why should I be afraid when the days turn bad, when the guilt that dogs my heels closes in around me?
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the riddle itself, and it is hard on purpose. The question is simple: why fear "days of evil" (the bad times, which most readings take as old age, poverty, or the day of death)? The second half is dense: "the iniquity of my heels". The KJV and ASV keep it literally, and so does the literal layer, but English cannot say what it means. Rashi and Metzudat David explain: it is the sins that a man treads on with his heel, the ones he treats as light, which in the end convict him. Ibn Ezra reads it as the crooked path walked while gathering wealth. YLT and BBE take another road and read ʿăqēbay as "my supplanters", from ʿāqēb, the root of Jacob's name, and put the danger in other people. The Hebrew allows both, and the pun on Jacob, the heel-grabber, is probably alive.

Be careful about the tone: the speaker is not afraid. The question is rhetorical and the answer is held back until verse 16. The singer sets the problem in front of the crowd: if my wrongs are all around me, why am I calm, while the rich are not? The KJV's "shall compass me about" turns the Hebrew present into a future and adds a "when" that the Hebrew leaves out.

philological_notes.note: 'The iniquity of my heels'. Read as wrongs trodden underfoot and thought trivial (Rashi, Metzudat David), as a crooked path (Ibn Ezra), or, with the same consonants vocalized as 'those who trip me', as 'my supplanters' (YLT). The wordplay with Jacob (ʿAqōb) is plausible.
'It surrounds me': an imperfect with a doubled bet (dagesh), which Radak notes is written with a vav. The verb is of encircling, as a besieging army or a ring of enemies.

verses.translation_literal: Those who trust in their wealth, and in the abundance of their riches they boast themselves.
verses.translation_dramatic: They put their trust in their wealth. They swell with pride over the sheer abundance of their riches.
verses.directors_commentary:
From the riddle the poet turns to the people it is about: the "trusters" (habbōṭḥîm). The grammar is loose on purpose. The participle "those who trust" is left standing at the start of the sentence, with no verb to govern it, so it hangs in the air like a pointing finger. Ibn Ezra says it is the start of a new thought; Meiri reads it as an address, "you who trust"; Metzudat David says that if even I fear, how much more should they. In performance, the line should be delivered at the rich, not about them.

Two words matter. Ḥayil means strength, army, and by extension wealth, in the way the English word "force" can mean money and might; Ibn Ezra cites "he made me this wealth" (Deut 8:17). Wealth was a trust placed in something physical, as security stood on a stone wall. The second verb, yithallālû, is the reflexive of the verb for praising: they praise themselves. The KJV's "boast themselves in the multitude of their riches" is close; the YLT's "do shew themselves foolish" reads the same verb as the homograph meaning "to act madly", a reading the root also allows. Compare the praise that Israel gives to the LORD with the verb used for how the rich praise their own money.

philological_notes.note: 'Their wealth': ḥayil is strength, an army, and so resources. Metzudat Zion and Ibn Ezra gloss it as 'their riches'; Ibn Ezra compares Deut 8:17.
A reflexive of the verb 'to praise': 'they praise themselves, they boast'. The same root can mean 'to act madly' in the intensive stem, which YLT hears here.

verses.translation_literal: A brother — he will not ever ransom, a man; he will not give to God his ransom-price.
verses.translation_dramatic: No man can buy back his brother. No man can lay down before God the price of a life.
verses.directors_commentary:
Here is the law of the ransom at the centre of the psalm. In the ancient Near East a life could sometimes be bought: Exodus 21:30 lets a man whose ox has killed pay a "ransom" (kōper) for his own life, and the same law shows what money cannot buy, for Numbers 35:31 forbids a ransom for a murderer. The poet takes this ordinary idiom of kinship and pushes it to the limit: the closest person, a brother, who is bound by custom to redeem you from debt or slavery (Leviticus 25:48), cannot redeem you from death, and you cannot pay God directly either.

The Hebrew is emphatic in a way the KJV only half carries: pādōh yipdeh, the verb doubled (an infinitive absolute), is a flat "not at all, ever". The KJV's "None of them can by any means redeem his brother" adds "of them" and a modal "can" that is not there; the Hebrew has just "will not". Its word order, with "brother" thrown to the front, makes the brother the thing under the hammer. The word for ransom, kōper, is the legal price that covers a life; the verb pdh, "redeem", is the commercial term. The poem uses the language of the marketplace to say the marketplace ends here. Note, too, that the speaker uses ʾĕlōhîm, not the divine name, as the psalms of Book II usually do (the Elohistic Psalter).

philological_notes.note: A verb doubled with its absolute infinitive, which intensifies the negation: 'he will certainly not redeem'. The verb is the commercial term for buying back a person or property.
'His ransom': kōper is the price that covers a life under law (Exod 21:30). Metzudat Zion glosses it as 'the redemption of his soul'.

verses.translation_literal: And costly [is] the ransom of their life, and it ceases for ever.
verses.translation_dramatic: For the price of a life is more than any hand can pay. It is a price that has stopped being named, and will not be named again.
verses.directors_commentary:
This verse is a hinge, and it is a parenthesis: it explains verse 8 (no man can ransom another or pay God his kōper) and runs straight on into verse 10 ('that he should live on for ever and never see the Pit'). Read it as one breath with both.

Two words decide the sense. Nefesh is not the 'soul' of the KJV, a detachable spirit; it is the life of the whole person, the breath and the throat, and the sentence is about keeping a man alive. And yēqar, 'costly', is also the Hebrew for 'rare', as in 1 Samuel 3:1, 'the word of the LORD was rare (yāqār)': Meiri and Metzudat Zion hear that sense here, so that the ransom is not merely dear but not to be found. The last word, wĕḥādal lĕʿôlām, can be read two ways. Radak takes it as the thing that ceases: the ransom, or the hope of it, is gone for ever, since a man cannot be kept alive for ever and never see the grave; the KJV and ASV take it this way ('it ceaseth', 'it faileth for ever'). Rashi, commenting on the previous verse, takes the one who would pay as the subject: he gives up the attempt for ever, because the price outruns all his wealth. The Hebrew allows both, and the stress falls the same either way.

The ancient frame is the kōper, the payment that buys a life out of a death sentence or a debt (Exodus 21:30). The psalmist's point is a bitter one for those who trust in wealth: money buys everything except the one thing that is owed to God, and no price exists for it. Play it flat, as a fact that closes a door.

philological_notes.note: 'And it is costly', and also 'it is rare, hard to come by'. Meiri and Metzudat Zion compare 1 Samuel 3:1; Rashi, following Menachem, takes it as 'withheld, kept back', so that the ransom is simply withheld. The KJV's 'precious' blurs these into one general idea of value.

'And it ceases / he gives up'. If the subject is the redemption or the thing itself, it has ceased for ever, as Radak reads it, and as the ASV ('faileth') and KJV ('ceaseth') render it. If the subject is the would-be redeemer, he leaves off paying, as Rashi reads it on verse 8. The word looks forward to verse 10.
'Their life, their self'. The KJV's 'soul' carries later ideas of a separate spirit; here it is the living person whose death is at stake.

verses.translation_literal: That he should live on still to perpetuity, [that] he not see the pit.
verses.translation_dramatic: He wants to go on living, always; he wants never to look down into the pit.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the wish that no money can fulfil, put as the content of the unpaid ransom: that the rich man may live on for ever and never see the Pit. Metzudat David and Meiri both read it as irony, a question: is he really going to live for ever and never see the grave? The verb is a jussive (wîḥî, "let him live"), which gives the sense of a wish or a purpose: this is what the money is meant to buy.

The KJV's "corruption" for šaḥat is a famous mistranslation that came into English through the Greek Bible, which read the word as diaphthora ("decay"). The Hebrew word is šaḥat, which most lexicons derive from šûaḥ, "to sink" or "to dig a pit"; Metzudat Zion glosses it simply as "the pit of the grave". The difference matters: "corruption" suggests the body rotting, whereas a pit is a place, a hole in the earth, and later in this psalm (verse 15) the poet will speak of Sheol. The Targum, a late reading, renders it as Gehenna, but that is the language of a later age. Say "pit".

philological_notes.note: 'The pit': the grave, a place of descent. The KJV 'corruption' follows the Greek (diaphthora) rather than the Hebrew, which most lexicons connect with sinking or digging a pit (BDB). Metzudat Zion: 'the pit of the grave'.
'To perpetuity': the same root as the choirmaster of verse 1 (lamnaṣṣēaḥ), so the psalm opens and closes this section on a word of permanence.

verses.translation_literal: For he sees: wise ones die; together the fool and the brutish perish, and they leave to others their wealth.
verses.translation_dramatic: For anyone can see it: the wise die, and the fool and the dullard die alongside them, and every last one leaves his wealth to strangers.
verses.directors_commentary:
Here is the argument, and it is the oldest observation in wisdom literature: death makes no distinction. The subject of "he sees" is anyone, the rich man or the listener, so the line reads "anyone can see". Ecclesiastes 2:16 says the same of the wise and the fool, who are not remembered for ever. The poet piles up three words for the foolish: "fool" (kĕsîl, the thick-headed), "brutish" (baʿar, from the word for cattle, so "beast-like") and, implicitly, the rich man himself. Metzudat Zion glosses baʿar as simply "fool"; the KJV's "brutish person" keeps the animal root. That animal image returns in the refrain of verses 13 and 21, where mortal man is "like the beasts that perish".

Note the verbs. The wise "die" (mût), but the fool and the brute "perish" (ʾābad), a verb of being lost. Rashi and Meiri use this: death of the body for the wise, loss for the fool; the poem leaves it as a hint, not a doctrine. The KJV's "likewise" renders yaḥad, "together", which has been the keyword since verse 3. The last clause is the sting: they "leave to others" (laʾăḥērîm) their wealth, the word "others" meaning heirs, or strangers, or anyone but the one who earned it. The word for wealth, ḥêlām, repeats verse 7: the thing they trusted passes to someone else.

philological_notes.note: 'The fool and the brutish': baʿar is related to baʿîr, 'cattle', so the word means 'beast-like, stupid'. Metzudat Zion glosses it as 'fool'.
The wise 'die', the fool and the brute 'perish'. Rashi and Meiri see a distinction between the death of the body and being lost entirely; it is a hint, not a stated doctrine.

verses.translation_literal: Their inner part [is] their houses for ever, their dwelling places to generation and generation; they have called by their names upon lands.
verses.translation_dramatic: Inwardly they believe their houses will stand for ever, their dwellings from one generation to the next. They have even stamped their own names across the land.
verses.directors_commentary:
This verse is the hardest in the passage. The text says literally "their inner part, their houses, for ever", and the verse has no verb in its first half. The Masoretic reading, qirbām, "their inner part", makes it a statement about their thoughts: what they hold inside is that their houses are for ever (Rashi, Radak, Meiri, the KJV's "their inward thought"). Ibn Ezra records two other readings, among them that the word is a swapped spelling of qibrām, "their grave", so that their graves are their houses for ever, which is what BBE prints. The Hebrew then says a bitter thing: the one house they will certainly keep is the tomb. Both readings produce irony, and the performance can let them both sound.

The pair "houses" and "dwelling places" is a standard poetic pair: bāttêmô has an archaic suffix, a deliberately old-fashioned ending, as in the style of heroic speech. The last clause is a status marker: to "call by name upon lands" is to register an estate under one's own name, as men do when they put their names on a city or a field (Genesis 4:17, where Cain names a city for his son; Rashi cites it, and adds Antiochus and Seleucus, who named cities Antioch and Seleucia). Land, in the ancient world, was the proof of lineage: an inheritance that stayed in a family's name. The KJV's "call their lands after their own names" reverses the Hebrew, which says they call their names "upon" (ʿălê) the lands, a legal formula of ownership, as when a name is called over something to claim it. The poem's point is the contrast: they have named the land, but the land (ʾădāmâ, the same word as the ground in Adam's name) will outlast the name.

philological_notes.note: 'Their inward part': read as 'their inner thought' by Rashi, Radak and Meiri. Ibn Ezra reports a reading as a swapped spelling of qibrām, 'their grave', which BBE follows ('the place of the dead is their house').
'Their houses': the old poetic suffix -mô instead of -hem, a mark of elevated style.

'They called by their names on lands': to name an estate after oneself, a claim of ownership and memorial. Rashi compares Genesis 4:17 and the Seleucid city names; Metzudat David reads it as saying 'this is the land of so-and-so'.

verses.translation_literal: And Adam in honor does not lodge; he is likened like the beasts, they are silenced.
verses.translation_dramatic: But a man in all his honor does not stay the night. He is made like the beasts, and like the beasts he falls silent.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the refrain of the psalm; it returns in verse 21 with 'does not lodge' (bal yālîn) changed to 'does not understand' (wĕlō yāvîn). Here the lodging image carries the force. Yālîn is 'spend the night', and the ancient world knew that a guest is a short-term resident. Radak reads death as a lodging, as it is also called sleep. One reading, which Ibn Ezra reports from others and backs with Psalm 25:13, 'his soul shall lodge in goodness', has bikār as the man's honor in the sense of his wealth, and the line says that wealth does not stay the night with him. Either way the man in his finery is a traveler who will not get past the first night.

The KJV's 'abideth not' is right in sense but loses the picture of a guest leaving. The word nimšal, 'he is likened', is built on the same root as māšāl, the 'proverb' of verse 5: the man who will not learn the parable becomes one, a saying about what happens to people. Then comes the last word, nidmû, which is deliberately double. Rashi derives it from dĕmāmāh, 'silence': the beasts fall silent, and so does the man. Radak says it either means 'likeness', a doubling of nimšal, or 'cut off' (nikrĕtû), as animals are cut off in death; Ibn Ezra also reads 'cut off'. The KJV's 'beasts that perish' picks only one of these, and turns a quiet word into a loud one. Let the actor drop the voice on the final word.

philological_notes.note: 'Does not lodge, does not spend the night'. Bal is the poetic negative. Radak reads the lodging as death, which is also called sleep; Ibn Ezra compares Psalm 25:13 for the verb.
'He is likened'. It shares its root with māšāl, the proverb of verse 5, and Rashi simply glosses it 'from the language of māšāl'. The man becomes an object lesson.

A word with more than one root and so more than one sense: 'they are silenced' (from dmm, Rashi's דממה), 'they are alike' (from dmh, Radak's דמיון, which doubles nimšal), or 'they are cut off' (from dmh II, Radak's and Ibn Ezra's נכרתו). The versions split accordingly: 'perish' (KJV), 'cut off' (YLT), 'comes to an end' (BBE).

verses.translation_literal: This [is] their way, folly to them; and after them, [people] with their mouth take delight. Selah.
verses.translation_dramatic: So this is the road they walk: a road of folly, and every step of it their own. And when they are gone, the ones who come after will still be at it, praising the very words that led them there. Selah.
verses.directors_commentary:
Here the voice turns from the cold fact to the cause. The speaker points, 'this', at the whole parade of the wealthy as if it were passing in the street. כסל has two meanings that Hebrew keeps side by side: 'folly' (so Rashi, Radak, Meiri, and the KJV's 'folly') and 'confidence, trust' (Job 8:14; 31:24). The line gives you both: this is the way of men who trust themselves, and that trust is folly. The little form למו, an archaic poetic 'to them', adds a bitter note, 'theirs and theirs alone'.

The second line is disputed, so do not play it too certainly. 'After them' may mean their descendants, as in Ibn Ezra, Radak and Metzudat David, who delight in 'their mouth', their boasting words. Rashi hears something more pointed: 'they will talk about them', the next generation retelling what befell their forebears. Meiri reads 'their end', with the fortune cut short and a prayer murmured only by the mouth. The KJV's 'approve their sayings' picks the first reading and harmonizes it, adding 'sayings', which the Hebrew only implies by 'mouth'. BBE's 'silver' and 'gold' come from a different reading and appear nowhere in the Hebrew. Selah is a marker in the musical text whose meaning is lost, and it is best treated as a pause in the music: let the strings answer.

philological_notes.note: 'Folly' (Rashi, Radak, Meiri; compare Eccl 7:25) or 'trust, confidence' (Job 8:14; Ps 78:7). The pun is deliberate, or at least both senses were audible: their confidence is their folly.

'Take pleasure in, approve' (Ibn Ezra, Radak, Metzudat David); Rashi alternatively derives it from הרצאת דברים, 'recounting'. The two readings split the ancient translators on what the descendants do with their fathers' words.

verses.translation_literal: Like sheep for Sheol they are set; Death shepherds them; and the upright rule over them at the morning; and their form is for Sheol to wear away, from a lofty abode to it.
verses.translation_dramatic: Like a flock they are driven, and the fold they are driven to is Sheol. Death himself takes the crook, and he is their shepherd now. They go in, one behind another, and the pasture has no end. But morning is coming, and when it breaks it is the upright who stand over them. All that shape and splendor of theirs is made for the dark to chew away, and what was once a high house for each of them is a house no longer.
verses.directors_commentary:
The verse turns on one verb used with a bitter twist. רָעָה is the ordinary word for shepherding, the tender work of leading a flock to pasture, and here the shepherd is Death and the pasture is Sheol. Rashi hears a second verb behind the same consonants, 'to break', as in Jeremiah 15:12, and Metzudat Zion glosses it 'breaks them'. The audience would have heard both: leading and crushing. Play the line with a soft, almost pastoral voice that curdles at the last word. Notice also that it is the rich, who a verse ago walked in confidence, who are now the sheep: in the ancient world a flock's whole fate belonged to the one holding the staff.

The KJV obscures a good deal. It makes Sheol 'the grave', as if only a burial pit were in view, where the Hebrew names the underworld itself. 'Death shall feed on them' loses the shepherd image completely, since feeding is not leading, and 'their beauty shall consume in the grave from their dwelling' is not an English sentence anyone can follow. The Hebrew says that their form (צוּרָם) is for Sheol to wear down (לְבַלּוֹת), the word used of garments and bodies that wear out. The final phrase מִזְּבֻל לוֹ is truly hard: זְבֻל is a lofty dwelling, the word used of Solomon's temple in 1 Kings 8:13, and the commentators split on whose dwelling it is. The upright 'ruling' at the morning is not a coup. Morning is the hour of judgment and of rescue in Israel's poetry, the hour when the night's terror ends.

philological_notes.note: From רעה 'to shepherd, tend'. Rashi on Psalm 49:15 also offers 'to shatter', comparing Jeremiah 15:12, and Metzudat Zion glosses it 'breaks them'. The text holds both senses, leading like a flock and breaking.

The packet marks this word as a Qere/Ketiv case. Ibn Ezra reads it as the same as וצורתם 'their form', and Radak offers 'their form' or 'their strength'. Metzudat David and Meiri also take 'strength' as an alternative. I gloss it 'their form'.
זְבֻל is a lofty dwelling, as in 1 Kings 8:13 (Metzudat Zion). Whose dwelling it is and what happens to it is disputed: Radak and Metzudat David say the man leaves his fine house for the grave.

verses.translation_literal: Surely God will redeem my life from the hand of Sheol, for he will take me. Selah.
verses.translation_dramatic: But God. God will buy my life back out of Sheol's closed hand, for he will take me to himself. Selah.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the hinge of the whole psalm, and it should land like a door opening in a dark room. 'Surely' אך is a small word that works like 'but, yet': after eight verses of the flock marching down, the speaker steps out of line. פדה is the language of the marketplace and the law courts: to redeem a firstborn, to buy back a field, to free a slave. God is the buyer, and Sheol, which was a shepherd's pen, is now a hand that has closed on something that belongs to someone else. 'Hand of Sheol' is an old image for power; the KJV's 'power of the grave' is sound but changes Sheol, the realm, to 'the grave', a hole in the ground, and loses the hand.

The verb לקח, 'take', is the one used of Enoch, who 'was not, for God took him' (Gen 5:24); Meiri and Ibn Ezra both point there. Whether the speaker hopes for escape from death, for something after it, or only for a death that God receives is the great question of the commentators, and the Hebrew keeps it closed on purpose: Rashi says it is a life lived in God's ways, Radak 'he will make me die', Malbim a soul bound up in the bundle of life. The KJV's 'soul' for נפש is a Greek word on a Hebrew thing; נפש is the throat, the breathing self, the whole person. The actor should not play a disembodied spirit, but a man who is being held.

philological_notes.note: 'Redeem, ransom': a commercial and legal verb for buying someone back, used of firstborn sons, slaves and land. Sheol is the creditor.

'My life, my self'; the whole person, with the throat and breath, not a separable soul. Ibn Ezra reads it as the higher soul; Radak and Metzudat David as the self that must not perish with the body. The reading is the commentators', and the Hebrew does not decide it.
'He will take me': the verb used of Enoch in Gen 5:24 (cited by Meiri and Ibn Ezra), and later of Elijah. Radak glosses 'he will make me die'.

verses.translation_literal: Do not fear when a man grows rich, when the honor of his house increases.
verses.translation_dramatic: So do not be afraid when some man gets rich, when the splendor of his house swells higher. Let him.
verses.directors_commentary:
Now the speaker turns from himself to the listener, and the register drops from the pulpit to the whisper of a friend on the street. אל תירא is the plain 'do not be afraid', used elsewhere before an enemy, a famine, a king. Here the fear is not of violence but of envy and shame: the anxiety of the poor man who watches the neighbor's house rise and feels the world tilt. The psalm opened with 'why should I fear in the days of evil' (49:6), so this brings the argument back to its start.

The word כבוד matters. Its root meaning is 'weight', and the rich man's honor is literally his heaviness: the gold and grain and household that make him count. The KJV's 'glory of his house' is accurate but sounds spiritual; the context is a household and its standing, rows of servants, storehouses, a big door. ('Honor' elsewhere in this psalm translates יקר; the psalmist uses a second word here, and the difference is audible: one is value, the other is weight.) 'Made rich' in the KJV is a passive; the Hebrew verb is active, 'he grows rich', as if of his own doing, which is the psalmist's quiet point. The hearer is told not to fear a man who is only getting heavier.

philological_notes.note: 'Honor, glory' from a root meaning 'be heavy'; the weight of a household's wealth and standing. The word recurs in v. 18 with the possessive: 'his honor shall not go down after him'.

verses.translation_literal: For not in his death will he take the all; not will go down after him his glory.
verses.translation_dramatic: For when he dies, his hands close on nothing. He cannot take a single thing of it with him. And his glory, which he wore like a cloak and walked in like a king, will not go down the stairs after him.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the hinge of the psalm, and the verb carries it. Verse 16 said that God will 'take' (יִקָּחֵנִי) the speaker; here the rich man 'takes' (יִקַּח) nothing. The same root, לקח, is used for opposite outcomes: what God takes, the rich man cannot. Let the actor lean on the second 'take' with quiet relish.

The KJV's 'he shall carry nothing away' is accurate but flat. The Hebrew is blunter, 'he will not take the all', הַכֹּל, with the definite article, a single stroke that sweeps the whole estate. Ibn Ezra reads it as 'not even a part of it', comparing 'there is no all' in Numbers 11:6; Metzudat David says it means nothing at all. The second line is physical: כְּבוֹדוֹ, his 'glory' or 'weight' (the root means heavy), will not go down (יֵרֵד) after him into the earth. In a world where honor was measured by household, flocks and land, the audience would hear that prestige is the one thing that stays above ground when the body goes down.

philological_notes.note: 'The all', every part of it. Ibn Ezra and Radak read it as 'anything at all, not even a portion', Radak glossing it 'nothing from it'.
From a root meaning 'to be heavy', so honor as weight and standing. The same word appears in verse 17 as the 'glory' of the rich man's house.

verses.translation_literal: For his self in his life he blesses, and they praise you when you do well for yourself.
verses.translation_dramatic: In his lifetime he blessed his own soul, said to himself, You have done well. And they will praise you too, as they praise all who do well for themselves.
verses.directors_commentary:
This verse is a trap for translators, and the actors should know it is disputed. Its heart is the verb 'bless': he blessed his own self, congratulated and toasted himself, in his lifetime. Rashi reads a scene: the wicked man says to his soul, 'Peace be to you, my soul; no evil will meet you', a self-blessing, while no one else blesses him. The next clause is a second speaker's voice, a common cynical truth: people praise you when you do well for yourself. Whether the verse is a concession ('though he blessed himself', KJV, ASV) or a reason ('for he blessed himself') cannot be settled from the Hebrew, which has the plain 'for'. The KJV's 'Though' is an interpretation; I keep 'for' in the literal layer.

Note also the sudden shift to 'you' in the second line: the psalm slips from the rich man to the listener, so the crowd's praise is addressed to anyone who does well. The commentators divide: Rashi, Radak and Metzudat David think the 'you' is the wise listener who will do well for his soul; Malbim reads it as the man who invests in the next world. The KJV's 'men will praise thee' supplies 'men' for an impersonal 'they praise you'. Play it as an aside, with a thin smile.

philological_notes.note: 'Blesses', here of congratulating oneself. Rashi hears the rich man's own words: 'Peace upon you, my soul.' Radak says 'bless' means to add to one's good, so that the soul gets most and the body only what keeps it alive.
'And they praise you' (impersonal plural). Ibn Ezra says the praisers are 'the poor and the rich'; Radak and Metzudat David say 'the wise'.

verses.translation_literal: It comes to the generation of his fathers; for ever they will not see light.
verses.translation_dramatic: He goes where his fathers went, to the generation that waits below. They have gone, and they do not come back up, and never again will they see the light.
verses.directors_commentary:
The grammar of the first word is genuinely open, and the tradition splits on it. תָּבוֹא is 3rd person feminine ('it comes'), in which case it picks up the soul (נַפְשׁוֹ) of verse 19: so Ibn Ezra, who says it returns to the rich man's soul, and Radak, who says that very soul comes to the souls of his wicked fathers. Or it is 2nd person masculine ('you come'), addressed to the listener: so Rashi ('when you complete your days and die, you will come and see the generation of the wicked'), Metzudat David (when you come to understand) and Malbim ('if you come to the generation of his fathers, you will see'). The literal layer follows the 3fs reading, and the dramatic layer stays with a single rich man so as not to import a new speaker mid-verse.

The KJV's 'He shall go to the generation of his fathers; they shall never see light' smooths the plural in the second clause (יִרְאוּ), where the Hebrew shifts from one man to the whole line of fathers. The 'generation of his fathers' (דּוֹר אֲבוֹתָיו) suggests the company of the dead, the kin among whom the dead were gathered; Rashi instead sees the generation of the wicked suffering in Gehinnom. 'Light' here is the light of the living, and Ibn Ezra and Radak hear in it the light of God's presence. Play the final line low and slow: for a people who counted sunrise as grace, never seeing light is the real punishment.

philological_notes.note: Either 3fs 'it comes' (the soul of v. 19: Ibn Ezra, Radak) or 2ms 'you come' (the listener: Rashi, Metzudat David, Malbim). The reading changes who is addressed in the verse.
'Perpetuity, for ever', here an adverbial limit: 'until perpetuity'. Together with 'light' it contrasts the unending dark with the light the upright look to.

verses.translation_literal: Humankind in honor and not understanding; he is like the animals [that] are silenced.
verses.translation_dramatic: A man in his honor who does not understand is like the beasts. Like the beasts, he is silenced.
verses.directors_commentary:
The refrain returns, almost word for word, with one change that turns the whole poem on a hinge: 'does not lodge' in verse 13 is replaced by 'does not understand'. The first time, the point was that honor cannot keep a man; now the point is why, and who is to blame. The man who has honor and no understanding is a beast with a title. The psalm began by calling its hearers to listen, 'my heart's meditation is understanding' (49:4), and ends on its opposite. The sound is the same, and the difference is a single word.

The KJV's 'that abideth not' of verse 13 and 'understandeth not' of verse 21 are, to be fair, both near the Hebrew, but it also harmonizes both to 'is like the beasts that perish', which leaves out the pun on נמשל and נדמו that the refrain relies on (see verse 13). Rashi reads the final clause as meaning that the way of life is set before the man and he does not see it. Malbim goes further: the true 'honor' is the soul, and the man exchanges it for wind. The BBE repeats its verse-13 translation here and loses the clause altogether. Play the line as a gavel falling, quietly: the same words, now with a reason.

philological_notes.note: 'And does not understand': the replacement for 'does not lodge' in 49:13 and the pivot of the refrain. Rashi: the way of life is set before him and he does not perceive the good. Meiri: honor given in intellect, unused.
